content: Carrion's disease is an infectious disease caused by the bacterium Bartonella bacilliformis. It is transmitted to humans through the bite of sandflies belonging to the genus Lutzomyia. The disease is geographically restricted to certain regions of Peru, Ecuador, and Colombia, where it is considered endemic. The disease is named after Daniel Alcides Carrión, a Peruvian medical student who, in 1885, deliberately inoculated himself with material from a verruga lesion of a patient in the chronic phase of the disease. Three weeks later, he developed symptoms of the acute phase, thereby demonstrating that the acute and chronic phases were manifestations of the same disease. Tragically, he succumbed to the illness, but his self-experimentation established the etiology of the disease. In his honor, the disease was named Carrion's disease, and October 5th is celebrated as Peruvian Medicine Day. Later, in 1905, Peruvian microbiologist Alberto Barton identified Bartonella bacilliformis as the causative agent of the disease. Clinical Presentation Carrion's disease has two distinct clinical phases: the acute phase and the chronic phase. These phases correspond to the bacterium's invasion of two different host cell types—red blood cells and endothelial cells. 1. Acute Phase (Oroya Fever): This phase is characterized by sustained fever (typically not exceeding 102°F or 39°C), malaise, and severe hemolytic anemia. Transient immunosuppression is also a hallmark of this phase, which can predispose patients to opportunistic infections, particularly with Salmonella species. If untreated, the case fatality rate exceeds 40%, and it can reach as high as 90% in cases complicated by secondary infections. A recent study reported an attack rate of 13.8% and a case fatality rate of 0.7%. 2. Chronic Phase (Verruga Peruana or Peruvian Wart): This phase is marked by the development of a cutaneous rash due to endothelial cell proliferation, resulting in lesions known as Peruvian warts or verruga peruana. The lesions can vary in size and appearance, with three main types: miliary (1–4 mm), nodular or subdermal, and mular (>5 mm). Miliary lesions are the most common. Symptoms during this phase may include bleeding from the verrugas, fever, malaise, arthralgias, anorexia, and myalgias. Physical Examination Findings Skin: Pallor, jaundice, and rash. The rash may present as miliary, nodular, or mular lesions, depending on the size and characteristics of the verrugas. Eyes: Pallor and jaundice. Neck: Lymphadenopathy. Abdomen: Hepatomegaly and splenomegaly. Diagnostic Methods Acute Phase: Diagnosis can be made using a peripheral blood smear stained with Giemsa, cultures on Columbia blood agar, immunoblot, indirect immunofluorescence (IFI), or polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Chronic Phase: Diagnosis involves a Warthin-Starry stain of a wart biopsy, PCR, or immunoblot. Treatment 1. Acute Phase: The first-line treatment for adults is quinolones, such as ciprofloxacin. Chloramphenicol is also an option. In children, the recommended regimen includes chloramphenicol combined with beta-lactam antibiotics. A preferred regimen for adults is ciprofloxacin 500 mg orally twice daily for 10 days. For severe cases, ceftriaxone 1 g intravenously once daily can be added for 14 days. 2. Chronic Phase: Rifampin or macrolides are the drugs of choice for both adults and children. 3. Oroya Fever: The preferred treatment regimen is ciprofloxacin 500 mg orally twice daily for 14 days. In severe cases, ceftriaxone 1 g intravenously once daily for 14 days should be added.
